name: Sampang
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Sampang is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Huysmans 2007 'The Sampang word accent' (De Gruyter, pp. In its place the sweep found and read an open-access 2026 grammar sketch (Perry, Himalayan Linguistics Archive 15, sec. 2.3, pp. 7-8) giving a first-hand, weight-sensitive, non-contrastive stress description: nouns initial when all light, final when the final is heavy, later of two heavies, clitics unstressed; verbs penultimate/antepenultimate by syllable count with stress-attracting syllables; cues mainly pitch. Perry explicitly disputes Huysmans' stress minimal pairs (attributed in text to Huysmans 2011). Also read and found silent on stress: Rai 2009 (Nepalese Linguistics 24), and two Tribhuvan M.Ed. theses (Rai 2016, Rai 2018) in Preeti-encoded Nepali. Huysmans 2011 (Brill) remains unread (paywalled). All fetched sources

new_statements.quote: The verbal system of Sampang shows variable, but non‑contrastive positioning of the main stress. [...] in words with an even number of syllables, we see stress on the penultimate syllable, while in polysyllabic words with an odd number of syllables, it falls on the antepenultimate syllable. [...] Nominal stress in Sampang is relatively simple – clitics [...] are unaccented, so that accent always falls on the noun stem. Within the noun stem, if all syllables are light, stress falls on the initial syllable. If the final syllable is heavy [...] and the initial syllable is light, stress falls on the final syllable. If there are two heavy syllables, stress falls on the later one.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive word stress, sensitive to syllable weight and morphological category. Nouns: stress on the stem (clitics never stressed); initial syllable if all syllables are light (ˈmina 'person', ˈsjelama 'tomorrow'); a closed (heavy) final syllable after a light initial takes the stress (riˈram 'body'); with two heavy syllables the later one is stressed (saŋˈɡuŋ 'star'). Verbs: stress on one of the last three syllables of the verbal complex — penultimate in even-syllable words, antepenultimate in odd-syllable words (ˈimsa, ˈimsatsi, imsaˈtsina, japsaˈtsikana) — unless a stress-attracting syllable (closed, or ending in /ʌ̃/ or /e/, e.g. 1sg imˈsʌ̃, 1pl imˈse, imˈseka) pulls it rightward; fn. 12 formalises this as an Idsardi R2LIS system with left-headed feet and accent on the final foot head. Cue is chiefly pitch (trough on the stressed syllable phrase-internally, peak under focus), not length or intensity.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress-attracting syllables in verbs (closed syllables, syllables in /ʌ̃/ or /e/, including 1sg and 1pl suffixes) override the default count-based position. Perry says he could not reproduce Huysmans' stress minimal pairs (in-ma 'sell' vs in-ma 'hear' have the same pattern for him) and attributes the discrepancy to interaction of stress with intonation (a default stem-final high pitch that may be misperceived as stress). All judgements are impressionistic and 'provisional pending a thorough instrumental investigation'. CONTRADICTED by the dedicated study Huysmans 2007 (seen in snippets, pp. 155-160): weak stress accent, contrastive, 'predictable only for disyllabic nouns [initial] and temporal adverbs [disyllabic: final], but otherwise the position of the stress must be lexically specified'; verb minimal pairs 'inma 'sell' / in'ma 'hear', 'limma 'persuade' / lim'ma 'sprout'; i'si 'this year' / 'isi 'it is bad'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (noun stem incl. clitics; verbal complex); phrase-level intonation discussed separately and said to interact with stress cues.
new_statements.identity_note: Both descriptions concern the core Khotang-district Sampang (samp1249): Perry 2026 works on the Ṭāp Kholā valley variety (Phedi, Patheka, Khartamcha, Baspani wards); Huysmans 2007 p.153 locates his data 'in the north of Khotang'. An isolated Sampang dialect in Dhankuta (Cho 2020, per Perry) is not covered by either stress description. No separate glottocode for the dialects.

new_statements.quote: Nominal stress in Sampang is relatively simple – clitics (including possessive proclitics, together with case and number enclitics) are unaccented, so that accent always falls on the noun stem. Within the noun stem, if all syllables are light, stress falls on the initial syllable. If the final syllable is heavy (i.e. with a final consonant) and the initial syllable is light, stress falls on the final syllable. If there are two heavy syllables, stress falls on the later one.
new_statements.citation: Perry, J. Joseph (2026). A Sketch of the Sampang Language [HL Archive 15]. Himalayan Linguistics, Archive 15. DOI 10.5070/H9.61702 (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0).
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.3.3 Nominal Stress, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 10); verbal pattern in sec. 2.3.2, same page
new_statements.reading: Weight-sensitive lexical stress, non-contrastive. Nouns: initial stress when all syllables are light (ˈmina 'person', ˈsjelama 'tomorrow'); a closed final syllable attracts stress over a light initial (riˈram 'body'); with two heavy syllables the later one wins (saŋˈɡuŋ 'star'); clitics never bear stress. Verbs: stress on one of the last three syllables of the verbal complex — penultimate in even-syllable words, antepenultimate in odd-syllable words — except that closed syllables and syllables in /ʌ̃/ or /e/ (incl. 1sg/1pl suffixes) attract stress; the author formalises it (fn. 12) as an Idsardi R2LIS system with left-headed feet and the final foot head accented. Realised mainly by pitch (trough phrase-internally, peak under focus), not length/intensity. Author flags the account as impressionistic and provisional, and reports he could not reproduce Huysmans' stress minimal pairs (in-ma 'sell' vs in-ma 'hear'). This is the only first-hand stress statement read; it is a 2026 open-access sketch and should be the deciding source if Sampang is added to the catalog, with Huysmans 2007 (unread, paywalled) flagged as the earlier, partly conflicting phonetic study.
